$comment: The static origin's serving rules as DATA (Task 043, instruction 1).
This is not a second copy of deploy/nginx/default.conf to keep in step by
hand: tools/hosting-policy.mjs is the single implementation of the rules, it
reads this file, and deploy/tests/hosting.test.sh asserts that the nginx
config implements every class declared here. A file that merely described
the config would be a drift risk with nothing detecting it.
Every class names a set of paths, the Cache-Control to serve them with, and
whether the SPA document is the correct answer for a miss. That last field
is the one that is easy to get wrong and expensive when it is: serving
index.html for a missing hashed asset turns a 404 into HTML, which the
browser then tries to execute as JavaScript.
CHANGE_ME values are placeholders and MUST be substituted before a deploy.
deploy/verify.sh and deploy/tests/hosting.test.sh both fail on a CHANGE_ME

origin.note: The unprivileged nginx image listens on 8080, not 80: it cannot bind below 1024, and the image is built so that nothing needs root. The CDN reaches it over the provider's private link; the public entry point is the CDN, not this host.

edge.$comment: The hops in front of the origin, in order. Recorded as data because the security argument for the arrangement is entirely about which hop is reachable, and 'one public route' is a claim about topology that a diagram in a README does not check. deploy/k8s/frontend/ingress.yaml is the manifest; deploy/k8s/frontend/service.yaml (ClusterIP) and the `static-allow` NetworkPolicy are what make the claim true; deploy/verify.sh and deploy/frontend/hosting-config.test.mjs assert both.

hops.name: cdn
hops.responsibility: caches per Accept-Encoding, holds the certificate for the PUBLIC hostname, sets HSTS, adds the response security headers, redirects plain HTTP

hops.name: ingress-nginx
hops.responsibility: terminates TLS for the ORIGIN hostname, redirects plain HTTP, HSTS as an origin-side hedge

hops.name: static
hops.responsibility: serves the build with the cache and header policy in deploy/nginx/default.conf

hops.name: api
hops.responsibility: a different host with its own ingress; the frontend reaches it only through VITE_API_BASE_URL, which scripts/check-frontend-topology.mjs enforces

enforcedBy: deploy/k8s/frontend/service.yaml declares type: ClusterIP, so the pods have no address outside the cluster
deploy/k8s/networkpolicies.yaml `static-allow` admits the cdn-edge and ingress-nginx namespaces and nothing else
deploy/k8s/frontend/ingress.yaml binds the ORIGIN hostname, not the public one, so it is not a way around the CDN
singlePublicRouteToTheDocument.whyItMatters: A second public route to the document serves the identical bytes over plain HTTP with no edge policy: no HTTPS redirect, no HSTS, no security headers. That is the failure a second route exists to enable, and it is invisible until somebody uses it.

headersAreNotDeclaredOnTheIngress.why: ingress-nginx has no first-class annotation for an arbitrary response header. The two ways to add one - the `configuration-snippet` annotation and the global `more-headers` ConfigMap - are BOTH disabled by default since ingress-nginx 1.9 (`allow-snippet-annotations: false`). A manifest that depends on a disabled feature is a manifest that silently stops applying its security policy on a controller upgrade. The single copy of the header set is deploy/nginx/security-headers.conf, which the origin includes in every block that declares an add_header, and the CDN's viewer-request function adds the same set for the public hostname.

tls.note: The redirect is at the EDGE, not only at the origin. A user on http:// must never receive a response body over cleartext first and be redirected afterwards, and a redirect performed by the origin after the request already crossed the network is a response that was already observable.

$classOrder: EVALUATION IS FIRST-MATCH-WINS, AND THE ORDER BELOW IS LOAD-BEARING.
nginx resolves locations in a different order from a first-match scan: an
`=` exact match beats a plain prefix, and a regex beats a plain prefix too.
This array therefore mirrors nginx's resolution, not a first-match scan's:
- `document` is an `=` match, so it precedes everything.
- `source-map` is a REGEX (`\.map$`). In nginx a regex beats a plain
prefix, so it is evaluated before `hashed-asset` — otherwise
/assets/index-Ab12.js.map would be served as an immutable asset, which is
exactly the leak the class exists to prevent.
- every remaining `=` match precedes the extension class, because the
- `hashed-asset` is a plain prefix and precedes the catchAll.
- `spa-route` is the catchAll and must be last.
tools/hosting-policy.mjs asserts the catchAll is last, and
deploy/tests/hosting.test.sh asserts the running image agrees with whatever

cacheClasses.description: The SPA document. Names the current hashed asset filenames, so it must be revalidated on every request.
cacheClasses.why: A cached document references asset filenames the next deploy has already replaced. The result is a white screen on every hard refresh after a release.

cacheClasses.description: The origin's health endpoint. A static 200 served by `return` from the nginx config, with no filesystem access and no dependency on the build output.
cacheClasses.why: The deployment's liveness and readiness probes, and the image HEALTHCHECK, all use it. It must never be cached: a cached health response is a 200 that outlives the thing it reported, which is the worst possible answer from the one endpoint a monitor trusts absolutely. spaFallback: false because a probe handed the HTML document is a probe that cannot tell a working origin from a broken one. Added in Task 043A.

cacheClasses.description: Source maps. Not shipped, and refused rather than merely absent.
cacheClasses.why: A source map published by accident is a published copy of the application source. `sourcemap: false` in vite.config.ts is the primary control; the 404 is the second line of defence so that a future build flag change cannot leak it. Declared before hashed-asset because nginx evaluates a regex location ahead of a plain prefix one.

cacheClasses.description: Vite build output under /assets/, whose filenames carry a content hash.
cacheClasses.why: The bytes behind a hashed name never change, so the entry can never be stale. immutable additionally stops the browser revalidating on reload, which is the point of hashing. A MISS here is a 404, never the document: 200 text/html where the browser expected JavaScript produces an error that names the frontend rather than the CDN.

cacheClasses.description: The /version.json document the client compares against its own baked tag.
cacheClasses.why: This file's entire job is to report what the CDN is CURRENTLY serving. Caching it makes the skew detection report the answer to yesterday's question, so a stale bundle is never noticed. It is declared BEFORE unhashed-asset because that class also matches the `json` extension, and first-match-wins: the order is load-bearing, not cosmetic.

cacheClasses.description: The service worker, if one is ever added.
cacheClasses.why: A cached service worker pins a client to an old asset manifest indefinitely - the same failure as a cached document, one layer deeper and much harder to diagnose. Also declared before unhashed-asset, which matches `js`.

cacheClasses.description: Anything under the API prefix. Not this origin's business at all.
cacheClasses.why: The API is a separate host behind a separate ingress. If the static origin answers /api/... with the SPA document, a client gets 200 text/html where it expected JSON, and the resulting parse error names the frontend rather than the API. Declared before the extension class because a path like /api/v1/report.json would otherwise be served as a static asset.

cacheClasses.description: Vite's non-hashed outputs (favicon, manifest, web manifest, icons).
cacheClasses.why: Cached briefly rather than never, so a release that changes one of these reaches browsers without a hard refresh. These names do NOT change with content, so a year would be wrong. It matches `json` and `js`, so every exact-path class above it must come first.

cacheClasses.description: Every other path: client-router routes the server has never heard of.
cacheClasses.why: A deep link such as /projects/01HZY.../workspace is handled by the client router. Without a fallback to index.html it is a 404 the user sees, and no amount of client-side routing fixes it.

securityHeaders.$comment: Matches Task 037's SecurityHeadersMiddleware exactly. The API and the static origin must send the same policy: a stricter static origin and a looser API is not 'the API is internal', it is the weaker of the two that a browser enforces.
securityHeaders.Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self'; font-src 'self' data:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'
securityHeaders.$note: Strict-Transport-Security is listed here but NOT set by the API. It is a per-origin, browser-cached, irreversible-for-max-age commitment, and setting it on the API origin is a decision about the API's hostname that belongs to whoever owns the certificate, not to a shared header set. The static origin sets it because the CDN terminates its TLS and the commitment is part of the CDN's configuration.

precompressedSiblings.why: The origin image (nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.27-alpine) is built `--with-http_gzip_static_module` and is NOT built `--with-http_brotli_module`; `nginx -V` against the image is where that was established. So the origin can serve a `.gz` it was given and cannot compress to brotli itself, and a `brotli on;` line in deploy/nginx/default.conf would stop the container from starting with `unknown directive brotli`. The build still emits `.br` siblings so the edge can serve brotli without compressing anything per request. Only assets are precompressed: a `.gz` of index.html would sit at the top level where `location /` matches it, and `location /` declares no Cache-Control at all.

brotli.note: Brotli is negotiated at the edge, which is the right place for it independently of the module: the edge caches one representation per Accept-Encoding and revalidates against the origin far less often than a browser does. An edge configured for automatic compression will ignore the `.br` siblings and compress once, which is also correct - the siblings exist so that an edge configured for Brotli serves real files rather than compressing on the miss path.

compression.note: minLength 1024 rather than 0: gzipping a 300-byte file makes it larger and costs CPU on the hot path. Bundlers emit the same text repeatedly, so the win is entirely in the large files.

cdnVersionPinning.$comment: R6: the frontend rollback is a CDN version pin, not a redeploy.
cdnVersionPinning.procedure: docs/runbooks/rollback.md, 'Rolling back the frontend'. A pin is a pointer change, which takes effect at the next document revalidation; it does not rebuild or re-upload anything, and it is reversible in seconds.
